extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, researchers, research-integrity professionals, and informed general readers interested in scientific misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical criteria for identifying, triaging, and responding to duplicated or manipulated images in scientific articles, plus institutional and editorial practices to prevent and address such misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicated images
rubrics_metrics.description: The same image is used to illustrate different things (exact duplicates across figures or panels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that duplicated images can be honest mistakes (e.g., wrong file inserted) but are a common and recurrent problem; when found, flag to editors rather than publicly accusing authors. Look for identical images across different figures, panels, or publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identical/repeated images presented differently (rotated, inverted, flipped)
rubrics_metrics.description: Images that are identical or repeated but presented in altered forms (e.g., upside down, inverted) to appear different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These transformations indicate manipulation rather than simple reuse. Check for rotations, flips, contrast changes or cropping that preserve key features. Transformations are a stronger red flag for deliberate manipulation than simple duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-image duplications (cloning/repeated elements inside a single figure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplications within a single image, such as the same cell or element appearing two or more times in the same figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is hard to explain as an honest error (the interview: “It’s hard to believe that it’s an honest mistake when you see identical cells in the same image”). Treat within-image cloning as a high-probability indicator of intentional manipulation and escalate accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use image-analysis software as an aid, not as sole proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Image-analysis tools (e.g., ImageTwin) can find similarities quickly but are imperfect and should be supplemented by human review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software can find similarities in seconds but may miss obvious duplications and may also flag things a human would not. Do not rely entirely on automated matches; always visually inspect and interpret results before making allegations or reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish honest error from intentional misconduct cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Some image problems may be honest mistakes (file mix-ups, caption errors), while others show no plausible technical explanation and likely indicate wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for contextual clues (e.g., captions suggesting another image should be present, file-generation mistakes) before alleging misconduct. When referring cases to editors, avoid public accusations; phrase findings neutrally and let the journal investigate intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting & triage workflow for suspect images
rubrics_metrics.description: How suspect articles are identified and initially analyzed: reports often come from readers, reviewers, or platforms; initial triage includes checking author histories and following clues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common steps: receive tip or identify suspect paper; inspect images; check author list for repeat offenders; gather evidence and examples; notify editors or institutions with neutral language. Use community platforms (e.g., PubPeer) to document concerns but coordinate with journals for formal investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of paper mills and organized production of fake images
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper mills produce false articles and images, sometimes assembling unique fake images (AI/compound images) that are hard to recognize; many similar papers may indicate organized fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Red flags include many near-identical papers, formulaic wording across papers, and images that look artificially assembled from parts of other real images. Consider systemic drivers (e.g., institutional requirements to publish) and recognize that paper-mill output may be designed to evade simple duplication detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial and institutional barriers affect remediation (correction vs retraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions to correct or retract depend on investigation results; editors can be overwhelmed or conflicted (e.g., suspect is on editorial board), which slows action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all problematic papers should be retracted—honest errors may be corrected. Expect delays when journals have many cases or conflicts of interest. When escalating, provide clear documented evidence to help editors prioritize cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of peer review in detecting image problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers and editors often focus on plagiarism and methodological flaws, frequently overlooking image manipulation; rushed or compromised review processes miss problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume peer review detects image fraud—rapid reviews (example: 24-hour acceptance) or review by an editor-authored paper increase risk. Publishers should implement additional checks (image screening specialists or automated pre-checks) prior to peer review or acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication etiquette when raising concerns publicly
rubrics_metrics.description: How to communicate findings on public platforms versus contacting journals: public comments on platforms like PubPeer trigger emails to authors and can lead to backlash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When unsure of intent, avoid accusatory language; use neutral phrasing when notifying journals. Be aware that public commentary can provoke threats, doxxing, or legal intimidation. Consider private reporting channels for initial triage and reserve public discussion for documented concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and awareness-raising to improve detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Educating researchers, reviewers, and the public to recognize duplicate and manipulated images (e.g., using social media, lectures, consulting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer practical training (examples of duplications, how to inspect images, use of tools) and promote awareness among reviewers and editors. Publishers and institutions can hold workshops and hire specialists to screen submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional prevention measures and cultural factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions should audit lab practices, listen to junior researchers, and hire professionals to scrutinize images before submission to reduce misconduct motivated by abusive supervisors or perverse incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations include more oversight of labs, protection for early-career researchers who report pressure to commit misconduct, pre-submission checks, and creating roles for image-quality control within publishers or universities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community platforms and networks for monitoring and follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms like PubPeer and Retraction Watch serve as monitoring and discussion hubs and can surface problems for further investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage community reporting but corroborate claims with evidence. Recognize that posting on these platforms notifies authors and may lead to defensive or abusive responses; coordinate with journals or institutions when appropriate.
